question: What learning algorithms do sequence models acquire when meta-trained to infer unseen discrete Boolean functions from labeled examples in their context?

key_findings.claim: Transformers meta-learn several discrete function classes but show sharply class-dependent failures.
key_findings.evidence: A decoder-only Transformer trained on fresh input-function sequences reaches 100% on conjunctions and disjunctions, roughly 95% on 3-CNF/3-DNF, 91.5% on majority, 85.3% on 0-1 thresholds, 86.4% on integer halfspaces and 100% on nearest neighbor. It reaches only 53.7% on sparse parity (10,2) and approximately chance on harder parity tasks.

key_findings.claim: The parity failure is not explained by an information-theoretic shortage of examples.
key_findings.evidence: The paper contrasts the trained Transformer with Gaussian elimination and a task-specific feed-forward learner that solve parity with the same or fewer demonstrations, isolating a learned-algorithm or optimization limitation rather than sample insufficiency.

key_findings.claim: Minimal teaching sequences can make otherwise difficult functions easy, but the learned learner is distribution-specific.
key_findings.evidence: Transformers become nearly perfect after prompts deliberately chosen to identify the target, including DNF and sparse parity. A model trained on a mixture can switch behavior, whereas a model trained only on ordinary random examples does not exploit teaching prompts and vice versa.

key_findings.claim: Attention is helpful but not strictly necessary for much of the observed discrete in-context learning.
key_findings.evidence: LSTM, DSS, RetNet and Hyena variants often approach the Transformer on the Boolean tasks; Hyena is the closest overall, while larger differences remain for nearest-neighbor and regression-style behavior.

key_findings.claim: Pretrained language-model structure contains useful in-context machinery, but the strongest evidence still involves learned adapters or small synthetic tests.
key_findings.evidence: A frozen GPT-2 with learned input/output mappings beats a random frozen Transformer and nearly implements nearest neighbor. Prompt-only experiments with GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and LLaMA-2-70B are at least competitive with nearest neighbor for low-dimensional synthetic functions; only 100 random functions are evaluated per length and GPT-4's margin appears at dimension 15.

method.core_idea: Turn supervised learning itself into a next-token sequence task: each training sequence samples a new Boolean target and supplies input-label pairs so the model must acquire an in-context learner rather than memorize one function.
method.mechanism: Meta-train several causal sequence architectures across distributions of conjunctions, formulas, thresholds, halfspaces, parities and nearest-neighbor labels; compare held-out function accuracy, change the prompt distribution with teaching sequences, freeze pretrained Transformer blocks with learned bit adapters, and directly prompt large language models.
assumptions: Fresh functions and inputs prevent direct target memorization.
Synthetic Boolean families are informative probes of general in-context learning.
Accuracy on unseen functions identifies the implicit learning rule well enough for comparison.
The chosen architecture sizes and training budgets do not selectively disadvantage hard classes such as parity.

techniques.role: Forces the sequence model to predict labels for a newly sampled function from demonstrations.
Tests whether carefully chosen, function-identifying prompts change the learned algorithm.
Separates generic sequence-model learning from attention-specific behavior.
Tests whether pretrained Transformer computation is useful after learning only symbolic input/output mappings.

evaluations.setting: Unseen discrete functions from ten Boolean and nearest-neighbor families.
evaluations.metric: Held-out label accuracy as context length grows.
evaluations.result: High performance on conjunctions, DNFs, majority, thresholds, halfspaces and nearest neighbor, but near-chance on nontrivial parity.
evaluations.baseline: Nearest neighbor, empirical risk minimization, task-specific algorithms and chance.

evaluations.setting: Ordinary random examples versus minimal teaching sequences.
evaluations.result: Teaching sequences unlock near-perfect performance on difficult classes when the model was meta-trained to recognize that prompt distribution.
evaluations.baseline: The same architecture trained only on random examples or only on teaching prompts.

evaluations.setting: Transformer, LSTM, DSS, RetNet and Hyena trained under matched synthetic tasks.
evaluations.result: Several attention-free models are competitive, with clearer Transformer advantages on memory/retrieval-sensitive tasks.
evaluations.baseline: Decoder-only Transformer and explicit learning algorithms.

evaluations.setting: Frozen GPT-2 adapters and prompt-only GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and LLaMA-2-70B.
evaluations.result: Pretraining helps relative to random frozen blocks; direct LLMs mostly match a simple nearest-neighbor heuristic and GPT-4 modestly exceeds it in the largest tested dimension.
evaluations.baseline: Random frozen Transformer, nearest neighbor and fully meta-trained models.

limitations: All controlled tasks are compact synthetic Boolean problems, not natural language or realistic adaptation.
Most models are explicitly meta-trained on the same function family used for testing, so success is not task-family transfer.
Frozen GPT-2 still learns new symbolic input/output layers and therefore is not a pure zero-shot test.
Direct commercial-LLM experiments use only 100 functions per context length and cannot control undisclosed pretraining data.
Matching nearest neighbor does not show that a model recovered the intended symbolic algorithm.
Compute, hyperparameter and optimization choices may partly explain parity failures.
Accuracy alone does not expose which of several observationally equivalent algorithms is implemented.
failure_modes: A learner memorizes surface correlations in the meta-training distribution and fails after a prompt-distribution change.
Teaching examples are useful in principle but ignored because training never signaled that teachers choose examples strategically.
A high aggregate score hides chance-level behavior on algebraic structure such as parity.
Claims about pretrained LLM reasoning reduce to nearest-neighbor retrieval or contaminated symbolic patterns.
A small-model algorithm does not persist at larger dimensions, context lengths or model scales.
reusable_insights: Evaluate in-context learners across function classes with qualitatively distinct optimal algorithms, not one regression family.
Use teaching-sequence interventions to distinguish passive statistical learning from sensitivity to informative data selection.
Always include simple nonparametric and task-specific algorithmic baselines before attributing reasoning.
Treat meta-training distribution as part of the learned algorithm specification.
Report failure classes, not only averages, because compositional and algebraic tasks can diverge sharply.
open_questions: Which training distributions induce algorithms that transfer across Boolean families rather than within one family?
Can mechanistic interventions distinguish nearest-neighbor, empirical-risk and symbolic-rule implementations?
Why do parity functions remain difficult despite adequate examples and representational capacity?
How do learned algorithms change with model, data and context scaling?
Can strategically selected examples improve real downstream in-context learning without explicit meta-training?

competitive_landscape.title: What Can Transformers Learn In-Context? A Case Study of Simple Function Classes
competitive_landscape.difference: Garg et al. establish in-context regression, sparse regression, neural-network and decision-tree learning under distribution shifts; this paper broadens the controlled study to discrete Boolean families, teaching distributions and attention-free architectures.

competitive_landscape.title: What learning algorithm is in-context learning? Investigations with linear models
competitive_landscape.difference: Akyurek et al. construct and diagnose gradient, ridge and least-squares algorithms for linear regression; the reviewed work tests a wider discrete class but provides less mechanistic identification of the internal algorithm.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
competitive_landscape.difference: von Oswald et al. connect linear self-attention weights to gradient descent and curvature correction; this paper emphasizes empirical capability boundaries, teaching prompts and multiple sequence architectures.

competitive_landscape.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
competitive_landscape.difference: Olsson et al. trace a retrieval-like induction-head circuit during language-model training; the reviewed work probes function learning at the behavioral level and shows that attention-free architectures can reproduce many results.

novelty_assessment: The distinctive contribution is the combination of many discrete function classes, strategic teaching distributions, architecture comparisons and pretrained-model probes. It materially broadens early linear-regression studies, but most conclusions are behavioral and distribution-bound; it does not uniquely identify the implemented algorithms or establish natural-language transfer.
reviewer_notes: Read all 27 extracted pages, including per-class results, parity baselines, teaching-sequence experiments, architecture ablations, frozen GPT-2 analysis and direct-LLM appendix material. Four primary arXiv comparators were checked on 2026-08-23.
